title: What Happens to a Music Licensing Deal When a Brand Is Sold?

body_markdown:
In a licensing deal music rights do not automatically follow a brand when it is sold. The buyer may inherit permission to keep using a campaign, need the rights holder’s consent or require a new license altogether. The answer depends on which legal entity holds the license, how the acquisition is structured and what the agreement says about transfers and changes of control.


**A brand sale neither automatically cancels a music license nor automatically gives the buyer permission to use the track.** For rights holders, the immediate task is to separate existing permissions from anything the buyer now wants to do.


## Start with the legal entity, not the brand name


A consumer-facing brand is not necessarily the licensee. The agreement might name its parent company, an operating subsidiary, an advertising agency or another entity acting for a specified advertiser.


Before discussing consent, identify the exact contracting party and compare it with the acquisition documents. An announcement that “Brand A has been acquired” does not establish whether the licensed company changed owners or whether selected assets moved to a different company.


For example, buying all the shares in the company that holds the license is different from buying its trademarks, inventory and advertising assets. In the first transaction, the licensee may remain the same legal entity. In the second, the buyer may be a stranger to the license.


This is a U.S.-oriented review framework. Governing law and the specific transaction can change the analysis.


## In a licensing deal music rights follow the grant, not the logo


Transaction structure provides the starting point, but it does not replace contract review.


Transaction


What happens to the licensee?


Main music licensing question


Stock purchase


The licensed entity generally remains in place under new ownership


Does a change-of-control provision require notice, consent or another action?


Asset purchase


Selected assets move to a buyer that may be a different entity


Can the license be assigned, and does the proposed transfer satisfy the agreement and applicable law?


Merger


The licensee may survive, disappear or become part of another entity


How do the merger structure, governing law and transfer language affect the license?


Sale of trademarks or a product line


The brand moves, but the existing license may remain with the seller


Does the buyer receive any authorized music use, or must it obtain separate permission?


Do not assume that a merger avoids assignment restrictions. Language covering transfers “by operation of law” may matter, and courts can treat different merger structures differently.


Likewise, the words “successors and assigns” are not a reliable substitute for an express permission to transfer. They need to be read alongside the assignment clause and the rest of the agreement.


## Check the composition and master permissions separately


A music licensing deal for an advertisement commonly involves permission to use both the underlying composition and a particular sound recording. The[U.S. Copyright Office distinguishes these as separate copyrighted works](https://www.copyright.gov/circs/circ56a.pdf) .


The publishing-side license might permit transfer with a business sale while the master-use license requires prior written consent. Approval from one side does not resolve the other.


For each clearance, confirm the licensee, covered advertiser, licensed recording or composition, term, territory and authorized media. Then identify who has authority to approve a transfer. Where several publishers or owners are involved, check whether the existing administrator can give the necessary approval on their behalf.


An agency’s assurance that “the music is cleared” is not enough. Ask for the executed grants and amendments, not just a clearance spreadsheet or invoice.


Keep this review focused on the campaign permissions. A brand acquisition is not itself a transfer of copyright ownership, and a license to use music is not ownership of the music.


## Separate assignment, change of control and expanded use


Three different questions often arrive in the same email. Answering them separately makes negotiations more precise.


### Assignment: is a different company receiving the license?


An assignment concerns the transfer of contractual rights. The agreement may prohibit assignment, permit it with written consent or allow it for a defined transaction, such as a sale of substantially all the relevant business assets.


Read the exception closely. It may require the buyer to assume obligations, exclude specified competitors or apply only if the entire relevant business transfers.


Do not treat silence as permission. Some copyright licenses, particularly nonexclusive licenses, can be nontransferable without consent even when the contract does not expressly address assignment. Counsel should analyze the applicable rules before anyone confirms that a music licensing deal can move to the buyer.


### Change of control: does new ownership trigger a contractual right?


A stock acquisition may leave the licensee unchanged while still triggering a change-of-control provision. The clause might require notice, prior approval, an additional payment or another agreed consequence.


Check the definition rather than relying on the heading. Direct ownership, indirect ownership through a parent and a series of related transactions may receive different treatment.


Where the agreement contains no applicable change-of-control restriction, the rights holder should not assume that the acquisition creates an approval right. Commercial concern about the buyer is not, by itself, a contractual veto.


### Expanded use: is the buyer asking for more than continuity?


Even a permitted transfer does not necessarily expand the license. The buyer may want to replace the end card, introduce its corporate branding, run the campaign internationally or use the track across its other brands.


Those requests require a separate scope review. A music licensing deal that covers one product campaign does not automatically become a portfolio-wide advertising license because the advertiser now belongs to a larger group.


The most useful distinction is between continuing an already authorized campaign and commissioning new exploitation. The[core terms of a music sync license](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/music-sync-license-terms-every-rights-holder-should-negotiate) help determine where that boundary sits.


## Review the campaign, not just the contract transfer


A license may transfer validly while the buyer’s planned advertising still falls outside its scope. Ask for a concrete description of post-closing use, including which entity will publish the content and which brand it will promote.


A retained social account can be particularly misleading. Ownership of the account, video file or advertising creative does not establish permission to continue using the embedded music.


Check whether the buyer plans to keep existing posts visible, reactivate paid media, boost old posts, commission new influencer placements or create revised edits. Those actions may have different treatment under the grant.


Platform arrangements also need their own review. Do not assume a platform music library or the seller’s account permissions authorize every commercial use by the buyer.


For an existing music licensing deal, the practical question is not merely whether the same video remains online. It is whether the identity of the user, promotional purpose, distribution and timing remain within the permission already granted.


## Plan the gap between signing and closing


The acquisition may be announced weeks before closing, while campaign activity continues throughout. Establish who is responsible for music use during each period rather than treating the announcement date as the handover.


If consent is needed, determine whether the agreement requires it before closing, before the transfer becomes effective or before the buyer starts using the music. A promise to resolve licensing “after integration” does not fill a permission gap.


Where the parties want temporary continuity, they can negotiate a written bridge permission. It should identify the authorized entity, specific campaign assets, permitted media, territory, dates and any fee. It should also explain what happens if the acquisition does not close or the longer-term agreement is never signed.


Distinguish paid advertising from passive retention of historical posts. A limited archival allowance should not become an implied right to boost, repost or recut the campaign. Clearly drafted[sunset clauses](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/how-sunset-clauses-protect-music-licensing-revenue) can help define those stopping points.


A music licensing deal should not be backdated casually to conceal an unauthorized period. Document any retrospective permission expressly, including what it does and does not resolve.


## Decide whether consent changes the economics


A brand sale does not automatically create an additional music fee. Start with the existing agreement: it may already permit the transaction without further payment, impose a specified transfer fee or reserve an approval right.


Where a fresh commercial agreement is needed, price the permission actually being requested. A transfer preserving the same campaign, term and territory is different from a request for new markets, additional brands or a longer advertising run.


For a music licensing deal with ongoing reporting or payment obligations, identify who will provide statements and pay amounts attributable to periods before and after closing. If the license was paid through a fixed upfront fee, the brand’s sale price does not by itself create a royalty participation.


Exclusivity deserves particular attention. A buyer with a larger portfolio may seek protection extending beyond the original advertiser or product category. Do not let a transfer consent silently enlarge that restriction. Define the covered brands and category, then negotiate any broader limitation separately.


## Put the consent and obligations in writing


A short approval email can leave major questions unresolved. The appropriate document might be a consent to assignment, an amendment, a new license or a novation, depending on what the parties intend.


A novation generally substitutes a new contracting party and releases the outgoing party with the necessary agreement. An assignment and assumption does not necessarily produce that release. Make the intended result explicit.


The written record should address:


-


**Parties and effective date:** Identify the exact legal entities and the transaction being approved.


-


**Scope:** Specify whether permission covers existing assets only or also permits defined new uses.


-


**Obligations:** State who assumes payments, reporting, compliance and other continuing duties.


-


**Historical issues:** Address accrued amounts and alleged past breaches without accidentally waiving them.


-


**Limits:** Confirm which existing terms remain unchanged and whether further transfers require approval.


For any music licensing deal, consent should resolve the identified transaction rather than become an unrestricted permission for future buyers. Coordinate the document with both the publishing and master permissions so their effective dates and conditions align.


## Example: the same campaign, three different outcomes


Assume a beverage company has a one-year license for a recorded song in U.S. paid social advertising for one named brand.


**The buyer acquires the company’s shares.** The licensed company remains in place. If no applicable change-of-control restriction is triggered and campaign use stays within scope, the acquisition may not require a new music license.


**The buyer purchases the brand assets.** A different company wants to run the ads. The parties must assess assignment permission and applicable law; acquiring the finished creative is not enough.


**The buyer wants to add another beverage brand and launch internationally.** Even if the transfer is permitted, those plans exceed the assumed grant. The rights holder can negotiate additional permissions without characterizing the original license as automatically terminated.


The same music licensing deal can therefore remain effective, require transfer approval or need a scope amendment. The transaction documents and actual campaign plans determine which outcome applies.


## Frequently asked questions


**Does a music license end when a brand is sold?** Not automatically. It may continue, require consent or trigger another contractual consequence. Review the licensee’s identity, transaction structure, transfer provisions and any express termination rights.


**Can the seller promise the buyer that the music rights transfer?** The purchase agreement can allocate responsibility between buyer and seller, but it cannot itself create permission from a music rights holder. Any transfer must satisfy the license and applicable law.


**Can a rights holder demand a new fee after an acquisition?** Not simply because an acquisition occurred. A fee may be available under an express clause or as part of negotiating required consent, a new license or expanded use. Existing obligations still matter.


**Can the buyer keep old social posts online?** Only to the extent the applicable permissions allow it. Historical retention, paid boosting and reposting can be treated differently, so confirm the permitted activity rather than assuming all existing posts are grandfathered.


## Before approving the handover


Put the executed music licensing deal, transaction structure and proposed post-closing campaign use side by side. Resolve who may use the music, for what purpose, on which dates and subject to whose obligations before granting consent.


If the transaction involves a broader rights portfolio, incorporate those findings into the wider[music rights review for mergers and acquisitions](https://usethirdchair.com/blog/how-to-manage-music-rights-in-mergers-and-acquisitions) . The immediate objective remains specific: a documented permission that matches the buyer’s actual use.
